Impact of Walkability

Column

About Our Project

This project combines 2019 data from the Smart Location Database and National Highway Safety Administration Pedestrian Crash Data to provide a snapshot of how walkability influences multiple facets of life. We were most interested on seeing if city walkability is related to a number of things, including employment, average number of cars owned, average wages, and combining the Smart Location Data with the Pedestrian Crash data to see if there is a relationship between each. Links to each database can be found below.

U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Smart Location Database (with Walkability Index)

https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/smart-location-database8

National Highway Safety Administration Pedestrian Crash Data

https://www.nhtsa.gov/file-downloads?p=nhtsa/downloads/FARS/

Wage

Completed by Kyla Brannigan and Cheyna Warner

Column

Wage vs. Walkability

Column

About

This plot shows the relationship between walkability and worker wage concentration per US Census Block

Research Question: How is walkability related to worker wage concentration?

Hypothesis: I hypothesize that the distribution of worker wages will differ based on neighborhood walkability.

Conclusions: Worker wage concentration distribution differs based on neighborhood walkability. A Chi-square test was conducted to determine this (X2 (6) = 24,210, p < .001).

Specifically, the least walkable areas are skewed toward high-wage workers and underrepresent low-wage workers (though visually, this is hard to see).

Employment

Completed by Cheyna Warner

Column

How is walkability related to employment rates?

Column

About

This plot shows the relationship between walkability and employment rates. Only data for capital cities is shown and only some capital cities were included in the dataset.

Research Question: How is walkability related to employment rates?

Hypothesis: I hypothesize that unemployment rates will be greater in less walkable areas.

Conclusions: Walkability and unemployment rates have a significant, negative relationship.

Cars

Completed by Cheyna Warner

Column

Do households in walkable areas own fewer cars?

Column

About

This graph shows the relationship between walkability and number of households that own at least 1 car. Only data for capital cities is shown and only some capital cities were included in the dataset.

Research Question: Do households in walkable areas own fewer cars?

Hypothesis: I hypothesize that people who live in walkable areas will have fewer cars.

Conclusions: Walkability and number of cars have a significant, positive relationship.

Walkability and Pedestrian Crashes

Completed by Erika Davis

Column

What is the relationship between walkability and pedestrian crash data?

Column

About

This graph shows the relationship between how walkable cities are, and how many pedestrian fatalities happened in one year (2019). Data for walkability was originally by city, so was recoded to be by state, and not all states were represented in the dataset. According to the EPA, this data was only available in places that share transit data in GTFS format.

Research Question: Is there a relationship between walkability of states and the amount of pedestrian fatalities?

Hypothesis: I hypothesize that more walkable states will have less pedestrian fatalities.

Conclusions: There is no relationship between state walkability and the amount of pedestrian fatalities in one year. A simple linear regression was run to test this (t(19) = -0.17, p = 0.86).

Rural vs. Urban Pedestrian Crashes

Completed by Erika Davis

Column

Do rural or urban places have more traffic fatalities?

Column

About

This graph shows the relationship between whether a place is classified as rural or urban, and the total pedestrian car crash fatalities in one year.

Research Question: Do rural or urban places have more pedestrian fatalities?

Hypothesis: I hypothesize that urban places will show more pedestrian fatalities.

Conclusions: Urban places showed more pedestrian fatalities than rural places. A one-way ANOVA was used to determine this relationship (F(33377) = 173.6, p < 0.001).
